tone_statements.citation: Yang, Cathryn (2012). CLASSIFYING LALO LANGUAGES: SUBGROUPING, PHONETIC DISTANCE, AND INTELLIGIBILITY. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 35. pp. 113-137.
tone_statements.quote: p. 118: "The PLa syllable template is *(C)V(ŋ)T, in which one of 47 optional initials is followed by one of 9 obligatory rhymes and one of five tones, two of which have harsh phonation." ... "PLa basically retains the Proto-Ngwi tonal categories. PLa has three levels of pitch height in non-harsh phonation (*1, high and modal, *2, low and breathy, *3 mid and modal), and two levels with harsh phonation (*H, mid; *L, low)." p. 124: "The C cluster is also closest to Proto-Lalo due its conservative nature, e.g. its retention of the Proto-Lalo tonal system." p. 133: "The comparative method can identify contact-induced changes in CE-YA, such as the development of a contrastive low-rising tone identical to E Lalo's."
tone_statements.locator: printed pp. 118 (PLa tone system, sec. 4), 121 (Table 4: no tonal innovation listed for C or Core C), 124 (sec. 5.1), 133 (sec. 8); p. 116 for East/West Mounta…

tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone language, no word-stress statement anywhere in the paper. Central Lalo is said to retain the five-way Proto-Lalo tone system: three modal-pitch tones (*1 high, *2 low breathy, *3 mid) plus two harsh-phonation tones (*H mid, *L low); Table 4 (p. 121) lists only rhyme innovations for C/Core C and no tonal ones. Cited Central forms: C-LJ autonym [la̠²¹lo̠³³pa̠²¹] (p. 115), Core Lalo ŋa⁵⁵

tone_statements.quote: The CW-QY tonal system is a combination of contrastive pitch heights and harsh versus non-harsh phonation. CW-QY contrasts high, mid, and low level pitches. Tone 1 has two allotones, conditioned by the initial: high rising in syllables with voiced initials, and high level in syllables with voiceless or preglottalised initials. The low tone is realised as low falling in citation form, but is not considered a phonemic contour tone in the CW-QY three-level system. [Table 3-5: *1 High level 55 / High rising 45 after voiced; *2 Low, breathy 22; *3 Mid 33; *L Low, harsh 31; *H Mid, harsh 33]

sources.citation: Yang, Cathryn. 2015. Lalo dialects across time and space: subgrouping, dialectometry, and intelligibility. Asia-Pacific Linguistics A-PL 22. Canberra: Australian National University. 260 pp. (hdl 1885/95391, open access)
sources.tag: read: silent on stress

sources.note: No statement of stress placement. Ch. 3 gives phonological sketches of 15 Lalo varieties (Central = CW-QY, CE-YA, C-CJ, C-LJ [Longjie = Björverud's variety]) in terms of initials, rhymes, tone (3 pitch heights) and phonation (modal/breathy/harsh); syllable template (C)VTP and NT. The only mention of stress is incidental, p.39 (sec. 3.2, CW-QY): 'Following a stressed syllable, the syllabic nasal loses its syllabicity and merges with the previous syllable, as in yesterday /a²n̩³³/ > [aŋ³³].' a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/iambic/trochaic found nothing else.

sources.citation: Yang, Cathryn, James N. Stanford & Zhengyu Yang. 2015. A sociotonetic study of Lalo tone split in progress. Asia-Pacific Language Variation 1(1): 52-77. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/aplv.1.1.03yan

sources.note: Per the Crossref abstract: reports a tone split in progress in Lalo; 2,938 tone tokens from 38 speakers analysed by age, sex and education; the temporal extent of voiced stops' depression of Tone 1 F0 is increasing in apparent time, especially among women, while VOT of voiced stops decreases with education/Mandarin contact; a perception task with manipulated F0 shows listeners use multiple cues (consonant voicing, F0 onset..). Claims to be the first observation of a tone split while it is occurring.

Yang's C-CJ 'three pitch height contrasts, and harsh versus modal phonation') is not quoted anywhere we hold.
